clauses.reason: The order approves an amendment of the Code of Fair Competition for the Cotton Textile Industry and modifies the earlier approval. Its operative sentence orders that the amendment be approved (the held transcription prints these words as "said amendment bo and it hereby is approved") "and that previous approval of the amended portions of the Code is hereby modified to include an approval of said portions of the Code in their entirety as amended." Under section 3 of Title I an approved code supplied the standards of fair competition (3(b)), equity enforcement by the district courts (3(c)) and criminal liability for violations (3(f)), so the command had no operative effect apart from section 3. Section 2 of Senate Joint Resolution 113, approved on the date stated in the resolution as "Approved, June 14, 1935.", provides that all the provisions of Title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act delegating power to the President to approve or prescribe codes of fair competition and providing for the enforcement of such codes "are hereby repealed"; the resolution states no other effective date for section 2. The approval therefore ceased to operate on June 14, 1935. A. L. A. Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States, decided May 27, 1935, is recorded as a validity characterization (the section 3 code-making delegation was held unconstitutional; under the doctrine then prevailing an approval made under it was void from issuance), not as an end date, because no held record shows that the government cancelled or suspended this code on that date. June 16, 1935, the original two-year expiry of Title I, is not an end: section 1 of the resolution replaced that expiry with "on April 1, 1936", and nothing in the resolution defers section 2.

research_rationale:
Executive Order 6876 (October 16, 1934) approves an amendment of the Code of Fair Competition for the Cotton Textile Industry and modifies the earlier approval of the amended portions, under section 3 of Title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act. Applying the reviewed shared analysis: the code-dependent command has no own-terms end, no held record shows an earlier cancellation or suspension, and section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 (June 14, 1935) repealed the code approval and enforcement provisions, so the command ended on June 14, 1935. Schechter (May 27, 1935) is a validity characterization, not an end date. The text is an American Presidency Project transcription held as a provisional working text under the 2026-10-21 owner ruling; no certification is claimed.

The held-corpus search found no cancellation, modification under section 10(b), superseding code, revocation or suspension of this code before June 14, 1935. Held orders dated before October 16, 1934 that name the Cotton Textile code (for example Executive Order 6206-A of July 16, 1933, the final approval, and Executive Order 6858 of September 26, 1934) precede this order and cannot end it. Two held later orders act under this code without ending it. Executive Order 6878 of October 16, 1934 is issued \"under the Codes of Fair Competition for the Cotton Textile Industry, the Silk Textile Industry and the Wool Textile Industry\"; it directs the Textile Labor Relations Board to appoint a common chairman of the Cotton, Silk and Wool Textile Work Assignment Boards and directs those boards to study the stretch-out system and to submit before January 1, 1935 recommendations for a permanent plan for regulating work assignments, which \"if adopted in accordance with the National Industrial Recovery Act, shall become effective as therein provided\". Executive Order 6930 of December 27, 1934, issued under the same three codes, provides that the boards \"shall not be required to present before January 1, 1935, the recommendations provided for in Section 2 of Executive Order No. 6878\" and shall submit them within a reasonable time after that date. Neither order cancels, suspends, modifies or supersedes the code or this order's approval, and no held record shows that any board recommendation was adopted as a code modification before June 14, 1935. The WPA 1944 list shows no later numbered action on this code after October 16, 1934. savings.reason: Acts done and liabilities incurred under the Code of Fair Competition for the Cotton Textile Industry, as amended by this order, before June 14, 1935, and any fine, injunction or conviction already completed, are accrued effects that the repeal did not undo; the section 5 antitrust exemption for action already taken under an approved and effective code is likewise an accrued effect. The proviso to section 2 of the resolution names agreements and action thereunder and states no time limit, and the held text does not settle whether it narrowed that exemption for past action under codes. No held source continues the approval after June 14, 1935, and no held source shows a prosecution under this code continued after that date; nothing here continues the approval itself.

source_notes.reason: A. L. A. Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States judgment: the section 3 code-making delegation was held unconstitutional and the code provisions in question invalid; recorded as the validity characterization that applies to every section 3 approval, not as an end of this order.
